newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria government's honeymoon to be short-lived.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria government's honeymoon to be short-lived.

text.p: Celebrations of a big parliamentary election win for Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces will be short-lived as grim economic reality quickly replaces the euphoria.

The results of Saturday's election show a strong mandate for the new government to implement a package of tough reforms already agreed with the International Monetary Fund as a condition for new support to ward off bankruptcy.
"The honeymoon of the new government will be a short one," said Ivan Krastev, co-director of the Institute for Liberal Strategies think-tank.

The interim cabinet which took office after mass protests toppled the former Socialist cabinet in February has already won a large share of the public goodwill by stabilising the lev currency and bringing bread and petrol shortages under control.
The more unpopular measures are still ahead.
"Tomorrow some people will drink to our victory, others will drink to drown their sorrows and a third group because they usually do," said an editorial in Troud daily.
"But afterwards all of them will queue up for bread, cheese and ecus and they will count the few levs in their pockets."

With almost all the results counted on Sunday, the national electoral commission gave the UDF and its coalition allies 52 percent of votes, and the Socialists 22 percent. Three smaller parties will also enter parliament.
The election seals Bulgarians' rejection of rule by the ex-communist Socialists, a process begun with the election of President Petar Stoyanov on the UDF ticket in November.
The Socialists had controlled almost all of Bulgaria's nine governments since the end of one-party rule in 1989.
"This election victory shows that for the first time all age groups in both cities and villages have voted for the same political force," Krastev said.
He said young people who had reached voting age since the end of one-party rule had made a big contribution to the new political majority.

Support for the UDF is concentrated among the under-40s, while the Socialists' core support is among the country's two million pensioners, nostalgic for the low food prices and low crime rates under communist rule.
The new Euroleft movement set up by Socialist dissidents drew votes from young former Socialist supporters, and may attract more defections once the new parliament is formed.
Bulgaria has agreed to introduce a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime which aims to impose monetary discipline, reduce inflation and restore confidence in the national currency.
The new government must also privatise and restructure indebted, badly-managed state companies, and overhaul the collapsing banking sector.

UDF leader Ivan Kostov said the new government's four priorities would be carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files of public figures, and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.

Three smaller groups were set to enter parliament. The Union for National Salvation will bring monarchist organisations seeking the return of exiled King Simeon into parliament for the first time, in coalition with ethnic Turks.
They are joined by the Euroleft and the Bulgarian Business Bloc, led by maverick populist George Ganchev.
"For the first time the makeup of Bulgaria's parliament will represent a true national consensus," said Nikolai Kamov, political secretary of the Euroleft.
While suggestions for a grand coalition got a mixed response, the reforms have the backing of all political parties.

"Only the UDF has the will and the ability to govern the country. I think that there will be an unofficial majority which will suppport sensible measures by the UDF government and there will be a constructive opposition to the mistakes of that government," said UDF deputy leader Alexander Bozhkov, deputy prime minister in the interim cabinet.
